transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-06
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Sophie Alvarez (Redwood CSM), Janelle Morris (Aurora VP Eng), Devon Reyes (Aurora Platform Eng), Priya Singh (Aurora ML Eng), Alex Kline (Aurora SRE)

Summary: Quick weekly POC sync focusing on priority queueing behavior under microburst traffic, kernel selection tradeoffs for TTFT (first-token latency), and streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs. Agreed to run a kernel sweep on three sequence lengths and validate streaming warmup impact. Next steps and owners captured.

Topics: priority-queueing, TTFT, streaming handshake, kernel sweep, seqlen tradeoffs, fallback hedging, microburst mitigation

Action items (in call): see metadata action_items

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Tuesday. we'll kick off the 30-minute weekly, but i think we have about 50, so great. quick roll call?
[00:08] Janelle Morris: Janelle here, Devon, Priya and Alex on my end.
[00:11] Devon Reyes: yep, Devon.
[00:13] Liam Patel: Liam from Redwood, SE. I'll be nerding on kernels today.
[00:17] Maya Chen: Awesome. Sophie from CS is on as well. We want to start with the microburst bench results you sent, Janelle — priya, is that the 2pm traffic sample?
[00:26] Priya Singh: yeah that was the 2pm window, it's pretty typical — lots of short prompts, a few long chat flows. i tried to anonymize PII but if you see anything odd shout out.
[00:34] Alex Kline: noted, our SRE flagged a couple of tail spikes at ~400 rps for 30s.
[00:38] Maya Chen: perfect. Liam, can you take us through the benchmark headline?
[00:42] Liam Patel: sure. So we ran two configs on the dedicated pool: streaming enabled w/ small chunking and baseline non-streaming. Raw TTFT numbers — streaming median 85ms, non-streaming median 120ms. But the streaming had a heavier tail: 95th at 420ms vs non-streaming 95th at 330ms — likely due to handshake and microburst queueing. Also, kernel A (fused attention) is better at seqlen 64, kernel B (tensor-tiling) wins at 512, so it's a seqlen-dependent profile.
[01:25] Devon Reyes: hmm that matches what we saw — lower medians but more variance. Any notes on KV cache warm start? we sometimes see first-stream chunk hitting cold caches.
[01:33] Liam Patel: yep, we observed a KV cache cold miss penalty ~15-25ms on first token for certain model variants; that's more visible in streaming because the handshake path includes that first retrieval.
[01:42] Janelle Morris: are these numbers on the same instance type as our pilot? we are on g5x2 equivalent right now.
[01:46] Liam Patel: yes, same instance family and model repo. small mismatch on driver versions but we don't think it's material.
[01:52] Priya Singh: curious about the kernel switching policy. does Redwood automatically route by seqlen? or do we need to pin?
[01:58] Liam Patel: runtime will pick kernels by heuristics: seqlen, batch size distribution, and measured perf. but you can override via per-route hints. for deterministic workloads we recommend pinning for the pilot.
[02:08] Maya Chen: quick qualification — what's your success criteria for this sprint? is it TTFT under 100ms median with 95th under 350?
[02:15] Janelle Morris: that's close — goal is median <100ms for interactive flows and 95th <400ms for bursty windows, otherwise we worry about UX. cost is secondary but still important.
[02:23] Maya Chen: okay got it. let's talk about queueing — Devon, you mentioned you tried a priority queue prototype?
[02:30] Devon Reyes: yes, we shunted critical interactive requests into a high-priority lane, but under heavy microburst both lanes were saturated and priority still starved occasionally because we were using simple FIFO on the backends — no backpressure to top-tier.
[02:44] Sophie Alvarez: is that with connection pooling or separate endpoints?
[02:47] Devon Reyes: it's separate endpoints, same pool behind the scenes. we didn't get isolation at runtime.
[02:51] Liam Patel: sounds like you need queueing at the ingress level with rate loaning + admission control. Redwood can configure priority-queueing at the router; we can enforce token buckets per-priority and preempt lower priority requests when needed. that reduces priority starvation but increases lower-tier latency.
[03:06] Priya Singh: worried about added cost — if priority preempts a lot we'll spin more instances?
[03:10] Maya Chen: good point, we can do aggressive preemption but pair it with autoscale guardrails. also caching and batching knobs help reduce instance count.
[03:17] Alex Kline: can we do graceful degradation — fall back to a faster quantized variant when queueing happens?
[03:22] Liam Patel: yep, fallback chains are supported: route policy can move to a lower-precision/quantized model or to a smaller-faster architecture. this is often the sweet spot for SLOs. caveat: quality regressions need to be validated.
[03:34] Janelle Morris: on the quality point, Priya's team has a small eval set we can use if we run fallbacks — Priya?
[03:40] Priya Singh: yes, i'll share a 200-prompt eval and pass/fail thresholds. we'll need to see differences for short prompts vs long context.
[03:47] Maya Chen: awesome. time check — we have 20 minutes left. Liam, you mentioned kernel A vs B — can you sketch the sweep you'll run?
[03:55] Liam Patel: plan: run deterministic microbench for seqlen 64, 128, 512 across kernel A, B, and C (C is tiled + int8 path) with batch sizes sampled from your traffic trace. measure TTFT median/95th, CPU/GPU utilization, and memory footprint. also run microburst replays (30s bursts at 200-400 rps) to see queueing behavior.
[04:20] Devon Reyes: if you can include our real trace that would be great — not synthetic.
[04:23] Liam Patel: yes please send it; anonymized is fine. we'll plug it in for the replay.
[04:26] Janelle Morris: what about streaming chunk size? we tested small chunks and saw better median but worse 95th — is there a recommended sweet spot?
[04:34] Liam Patel: usual trade: smaller chunk => faster first partial token but more overhead per token and more chance of microburst amplification. Larger chunk reduces handshake frequency and amortizes kernel work, improving tail. For your workload we think 64-128 token chunking is a good start.
[04:48] Priya Singh: note that some of our UX flows expect immediate partials — can't sacrifice perceived latency.
[04:53] Maya Chen: two levers we can try: 1) maintain small chunks but add priority hedging so critical requests get preemptive slots; 2) increase chunk to 128 and use prefix caching to preserve perceived responsiveness. both approaches have pros/cons.
[05:07] Alex Kline: on-net security question: if we pin kernels or model versions do we need additional compliance approvals?
[05:12] Sophie Alvarez: not usually, pinning is a runtime config. for Private on-prem you'd go through our compliance pack but for Dedicated it's within the contract.
[05:20] Maya Chen: quick objection that came up during eval — OctoServe has an existing SLA we benchmarked against. Janelle, are you still evaluating alternatives?
[05:27] Janelle Morris: we're looking at them yes, mainly because of cost and region availability. but Redwood's streaming perf and dev tooling are attractive.
[05:33] Liam Patel: two notes: 1) we can run a side-by-side benchmark on your trace, 2) we have plug-and-play configs to reduce migration friction.
[05:41] Maya Chen: Anything else on kernel knobs?
[05:43] Liam Patel: one detail — for kernel C (int8 path) we saw occasional output artifacts on extremely long contexts past 2k tokens; not seen in your short-chat flows but worth validating.
[05:54] Priya Singh: we have a handful of long transcripts — we'll flag them.
[05:58] Devon Reyes: also to call out, our current infra does not expose per-priority SLA metrics — can Redwood provide per-route latency SLO dashboards?
[06:06] Sophie Alvarez: yes, we can add per-route/priority dashboards and token-level cost breakdowns. we'll scope a short dashboard template for you.
[06:14] Maya Chen: wrap up and concrete next steps: Liam runs kernel sweep and microburst replay using Aurora trace; Maya sends pricing + queue config; Aurora to send trace and eval prompts; schedule demo for streaming vs non-streaming side-by-side on 2026-10-15. Any objections?
[06:29] Janelle Morris: all good.
[06:31] Priya Singh: sounds good.
[06:33] Alex Kline: good.
[06:35] Maya Chen: ok we'll follow up with calendar invites and link to the benchmark sheet. Thanks everyone.
[06:39] (end)

Notes on transcript quality and artifacts: some words transcribed incorrectly (e.g., KV cache -> KV cash, seqlen sometimes spelled seq len). Speaker attribution auto-detected and may have swapped at a few short interjections.

Referenced artifacts: "microburst_bench_20261005.csv" (attached in CRM), "priority-queueing-examples.md" (will be shared), pricing spreadsheet link (sent post-call).

Recap (short): kernel sweep across seqlens, priority queue ingress + token-bucket preemption, streaming chunking tradeoffs, fallback to quantized models as hedging. Owners and due dates in metadata.
